scenes.intro: This is a demo of a closed-loop generative interface for learning. You bring your own study material. Gemini turns each topic into an interactive lab you learn by doing, followed by a short adaptive check that is sized to how well you are doing.
scenes.landing: The app opens on a landing page with the idea in one line: turn any document into lessons that adapt to you. Further down are the loop, the features, including learning by doing with thirty interactive components, and a plain statement of what is and is not claimed.
scenes.architecture: Here is the loop. Gemini reads the material once and writes a question bank, which is checked before use. For each topic it also designs an interactive lab from a catalog of thirty components; the server checks that every level can really be solved, and sends rejected levels back to Gemini once to fix. Then, in the check, a Bayesian Knowledge Tracing model estimates mastery after every answer. A PID controller turns the gap to the target into a complexity budget, a policy picks the scaffolding, Gemini writes the screen inside that budget, and a validation gate checks it before the browser renders it.
scenes.onboarding: Onboarding takes three short steps: name and level, interests, and a starting point. The starting point sets the model's first mastery estimate. Level and interests are passed to Gemini, so wording and examples fit this learner.
scenes.material: Next, the material. Ready-made sample packs are available, but here we upload a new PDF about the human heart, which the system has never seen before.
scenes.generating: The text is extracted, Gemini outlines the topics, and then writes twelve questions per topic, in parallel, at four levels: recognise, understand, recall, and apply. Every question is validated before use. The answer must be one of the options, and a fill-in-the-gap question must have exactly one gap. This takes about twenty seconds.
scenes.topics: Here is the result: topics with summaries and key points, all drawn from the document. Let's open the first topic.
scenes.lab_intro: Before any questions, the topic opens as an interactive lab that Gemini designed for this learner, with levels that get harder. On the right is a toolbox of key facts, and a panel that says honestly how the lab was made: the model, how long it took, and what the validation gate rejected.
scenes.lab_play: Each level is a real component to manipulate: labelling a diagram, sorting, matching, balancing, or running a simulation. There is a clear goal, hints one at a time, and feedback on every check. After two failed attempts a worked solution is offered. Gemini only writes the data; the components themselves are fixed, tested code.
scenes.lab_done: When the last level is done, the lab summary lists every level, and the learner moves on to the check.
scenes.first: Now the check, with at most ten questions. This learner is new to the material, so mastery starts low and the controller sets a small budget: a guided question with few options and a short nudge written for this learner. On the right, the gauge shows the mastery estimate, a panel explains why this screen was chosen, and under the hood you can see every value in the loop.
scenes.answering: As the learner answers, the mastery estimate is updated and the next screen is generated. Correct answers raise the budget, so the screens become more open.
scenes.wrong: A wrong answer pulls the estimate down, and the controller steps back to a simpler, more supported screen. Answers are always marked against the question bank, never by the language model.
scenes.higher: With more correct answers, the screens move up to recall, a fill-in-the-gap question, and then to apply, a new situation. The check stops after ten questions, or earlier once the mastery estimate passes zero point nine five.
scenes.summary: The topic summary says why the check ended, and shows the questions answered, the final mastery estimate, what was done in the lab, and the full trace.
scenes.gallery: All thirty components can be tried in the gallery: a projectile to aim, a scale to balance, a formula to tune with sliders, causes to link to effects, and many more. Each example was written by Gemini and passed the same gate as a live lab.
scenes.report: The progress report summarises each topic for the learner or a teacher: lab levels solved, the mastery estimate from start to now, the highest level reached, hints used, and the questions to review, with explanations. It can also be printed.
scenes.research: The original research testbed for linear equations is still here, unchanged. That is the part evaluated in the paper.
scenes.outro: To be clear about scope: the labs, the controller, the gate, and the marking are real and running live, and Gemini is called for real. But this general-content mode has not been evaluated. The paper's results cover linear equations with simulated learners only, and mastery here is the model's estimate, not a measured learning gain.
